transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, to be perfectly honest, I'm here because... well, my mind just feels incredibly foggy lately. It's like I'm trying to think through a bowl of thick pea soup. I've been working as a library assistant for years—mostly clerical stuff, you know, very routine, very organized work. I have these old cataloguing notes that I've relied on forever. I practically know them backward and forward, or at least I used to. But recently, I sit down at my desk, open up the binder, and I just... I cannot even keep my place in them. I'll read a line, and by the time I get to the end of the sentence, I've completely lost where I was or what I was looking at. 

And it's not just the reading, it's everything. I can't even seem to decide what simple thing to do next. I'll be standing by the returns cart, and I'll think, 'Should I sort these by fiction or non-fiction first? Or should I go check the front desk? Do I need to grab a pen?' Just the absolute simplest decisions, and I freeze up. I just stand there, completely stuck in this fog, unable to figure out the next basic step. It's incredibly frustrating, and, frankly, at sixty years old, it's embarrassing to be standing in the middle of the stacks feeling like I can't even manage the most basic tasks I've done a thousand times before. I just don't know what's happening to my head.
How long have you been experiencing this foggy feeling and difficulty with decision-making?

Well, let me think... it’s been a while now. I’d say... gosh, it really settled in about three months ago. That was right around the time I started getting everything ready to leave the library. You know, transitioning out, getting my affairs in order there. I had to start boxing up my personal things at my desk, and going through all those old files to hand over, and that's when I really, really noticed it. And it hasn't just been the fogginess, either, it's been this... this really heavy, low mood that just sort of hangs over me. 

And it’s been present most days. Almost every single day for those three months, actually. I mean, I'd wake up and tell myself I was going to finally sort out the transfer paperwork or organize my final handover notes, and then that fog just rolls right in and the low mood just anchors me down. Three months is a long time to feel like you're wading through wet cement. At first, I thought maybe I was just feeling sentimental or overwhelmed by the transition, because leaving a place after so many years, well, it takes a toll on a person, you know? You build a routine, you see the same faces, you organize the same shelves, and then suddenly you're packing it all away. But it didn't pass. It just turned into this constant, everyday haze and this awful down feeling that I just can't shake, no matter how hard I try to focus on just getting my desk cleared out.
Have you noticed any decrease in interest or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, yes. Yes, I have. I used to really look forward to my weekends. I’ve always been a bit of an amateur watercolorist, just landscapes, mostly, you know, little scenes from around town or places I’d visited years ago. I have this whole set-up in the corner of the dining room—the easel, all these little tubes of paint organized by color family, the heavy cold-pressed paper I like to order special from a catalog. I used to spend hours there on a Saturday morning, just mixing washes and watching how the pigment settles into the grain of the paper. It was my quiet time. 

But lately... gosh, most days lately I just sit at the kitchen table, maybe with a cup of coffee that's gone cold, and I look over at that easel, and I feel absolutely nothing. It’s like the color has literally gone out of everything. I’ll look at my old watercolor books, the ones I used to study for techniques—the John Pike one, and that big thick volume on English landscape painters—and instead of feeling that little spark of inspiration, that itch to pick up a brush, they just make me feel... heavy. Just so profoundly heavy and tired. I don't even have the energy to open the covers. It's not just the painting, either, it's like that with reading the Sunday paper, or even just sitting out on the porch watching the neighborhood. It all just feels flat and gray and pointless now, and I just end up sitting there at the table, staring at the wall, wondering where the joy in it all went.
Would you say that you have lost interest in all activities that you used to enjoy, or is it just some of them?

Well, doctor, honestly... I think it really is all of them. Everything. It's like I was saying about the painting, how I just sit there at the kitchen table most days lately, staring at my easel, feeling like the color has just been drained out of the whole world. And it's not just the watercolors. I mean, I used to love tending to my little tomato plants out back. I'd go out every evening, pinching off the suckers, checking the soil moisture, tying them up to the stakes with those little green twist ties. It was such a nice, quiet routine. But now? The weeds are coming up, and I just look out the window at them, and that same heavy feeling washes over me. 

It's the same with my old watercolor books, too, like I mentioned. I used to flip through them for hours, studying the brush strokes, admiring the way they captured light. Now, I see them sitting on the shelf, and they don't spark anything. They just make me feel heavy, like there's a weight pressing down on my chest, instead of making me feel interested or inspired. I used to enjoy cooking a nice Sunday roast, too—nothing fancy, just beef, potatoes, carrots, you know, the way my mother used to make it. The house would smell wonderful all afternoon. But last Sunday, I just couldn't bring myself to even go to the butcher. I ended up eating a piece of dry toast and going back to bed. It really feels like every single thing that used to bring me a little bit of comfort or joy has just been packed away in a box somewhere, and I don't have the energy or the desire to try and find it again. It's just... everything feels so terribly flat.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past three months?

Well, doctor, I haven't exactly been keeping strict track on the bathroom scale, to be perfectly honest with you, but... well, the eating has definitely changed. It's just like everything else I was telling you about, it just feels like too much effort. I actually have to consciously remind myself to eat during the day now. If I don't, I'll just sit there at the kitchen table and the whole afternoon will just slip right by without me even once thinking about food. 

My wife, she's definitely noticed it. She's been getting quite worried, actually. She'll make us dinner, you know, a nice bowl of soup and some rice, something warm and comforting—she makes this wonderful chicken and vegetable soup that I usually just love—but lately, she'll come over to clear the table and see that I've left my bowl half-finished. Just sitting there, the rice soaking up all the broth, gone completely cold. And she'll look at me, so concerned, because... well, before all this fog and heaviness started three months ago, I would never, ever waste a meal. I was raised to always clean my plate, you know? You just don't waste good food, especially when someone took the time to cook it for you. But now... I just take a few spoonfuls of the soup, maybe push the rice around a bit, and my stomach just feels sort of... closed off. The desire just isn't there at all, so I suppose I must be losing some weight, given how much I'm leaving behind on my plate every single night.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because my wife actually mentioned something similar the other day. She asked if my joints were bothering me, because I was just... moving so deliberately. But it's not my joints, doctor. It's just... everything feels so terribly slow. My whole body feels like it's moving through molasses. 

Even just walking down to the corner store, which is only two blocks away, mind you—I've walked it a thousand times, usually takes me five minutes, maybe ten if I stop to chat with Mr. Henderson about his hydrangeas—but lately, it feels like this monumental trek. I have to consciously tell my legs to pick up and move forward. And at work... well, I'm a library assistant, you see, so I do a lot of sorting, organizing the returns, filing the periodicals. It used to be second nature, just a quick flick of the wrist and the magazines were in their proper slots. But now, even just sorting a small stack of papers on my desk... it takes so much effort. I find myself just holding a piece of paper, staring at the Dewey Decimal number, and it takes me twice as long to process where it goes, and then my arm just feels so heavy when I go to put it away. It's not just the physical movement, it's the mental effort to make the movement happen, if that makes sense. It's like the connection between my brain saying "do this" and my body actually doing it has been stretched out and slowed down. I used to pride myself on being quite efficient at the library, you know, keeping the carts cleared, but now I'm just... lagging behind. Everything is just lagging behind.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could just go to sleep and not wake up?

Oh, goodness, no. No, doctor, I haven't had anything like that cross my mind. I know I was just going on and on about how terribly heavy everything feels, and how the color is completely gone from the world, and how I just sit there staring at my easel or the sorting carts at the library... but as far as not wanting to be here? No, I don't feel that way at all. 

It's more like... well, I just want to feel *better*, you know? I want to wake up and actually want to eat my wife's chicken soup again, or walk down to the corner store to see Mr. Henderson without feeling like I'm wearing lead boots. I certainly don't want to just go to sleep and never wake up. I mean, my goodness, I have my wife to think about, and my little tomato plants, even if they are covered in weeds right now, they still need me eventually. 

I remember reading somewhere, or maybe it was on one of those morning shows my wife watches while she does her crossword puzzles in the morning—she always does the daily one in pen, which I always tell her is incredibly brave, I could never do that—but anyway, they were talking about that kind of deep despair, and I just thought to myself, well, I feel terrible, absolutely dreadful, like a thick, wet wool blanket has been thrown over my whole life, but I don't want my life to actually end. I just want the blanket lifted off. So, no, no thoughts of not waking up. I just want to wake up and actually feel like myself again, if that makes sense.
Have you been feeling worthless or guilty about anything in particular over the past three months?

Worthless? Guilty? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I know I was just going on about how I'm lagging behind with the sorting carts at the library—and I suppose some people might feel terribly guilty about not pulling their weight at work, especially when it backs up the whole system. My supervisor, Mrs. Gable, she's been the head librarian there for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, and she's a very strict woman, always wants the daily periodicals filed the exact minute they come in from the mail carrier. She's certainly noticed I'm slower, and she's given me a few looks over her spectacles. 

But I don't feel *guilty* about it, because... well, I know I'm not doing it on purpose. I'm not being lazy, I'm just... stuck in this mud. I've been a hard worker my whole life, forty years of steady employment, so I know my worth in that regard. I know I'm a capable person underneath all this. 

And at home, my wife, she's just so wonderfully supportive. She doesn't make me feel worthless, not one bit. Even when I leave her lovely soup sitting there cold, she doesn't scold me or make me feel bad about it, she just looks worried. She just wants me better. So, no, I don't sit around feeling like a burden or beating myself up about things I've done wrong in the past, or feeling like I have no value to the world. I don't have that sort of inner critic yelling at me, if you know what I mean. I just feel heavy and blank. But my self-worth, I think that's still perfectly intact. I know I'm a good husband, a good person... just a very, very slow and tired one right now.
Would you say your low mood is mild, moderate, or severe most days?

Well, I suppose... if I had to put a word to it, I'd say it's moderate. Yes, moderate seems right. It's not a passing sadness, like when they canceled that mystery program on the television that my wife and I used to watch every Thursday evening—that was just a mild disappointment, really. But this... this is heavier. 

Most days lately, I just sit there at the kitchen table. We have this lovely oak table, round, fits perfectly in the breakfast nook. We bought it at an estate sale nearly twenty years ago, and usually, the morning light comes through the window and makes the wood just glow. But lately, I sit there, and it's like... it's like the color has completely gone out of everything. Even the oak just looks gray and dull. I'll have my coffee cup in front of me, and I'll look over at my old watercolor books—I used to love painting, you know, mostly landscapes, barns, that sort of thing—they're stacked right there on the little side shelf where I keep my supplies. And instead of feeling that little spark of interest, that urge to mix some cerulean blue and see what happens... looking at them just makes me feel heavy. Just terribly heavy. It's a persistent, thick sort of feeling, this mood. It just sits on me, day in and day out, right there in the middle of moderate. It's enough to keep me sitting at that table for hours, just staring at the gray wood, not really painting, not really doing much of anything at all.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Pleasure? Looking forward to things? Well... no. No, doctor, I really can't say that there are. And it's a terrible shame, really, because I used to be a man who found so much joy in the little daily routines. 

I mentioned my tomato plants earlier—Early Girls and Beefsteaks, usually. I always plant them right along the south-facing fence in the backyard where they get that really good, strong afternoon sun. Usually, by this time of year, I'd be out there every single evening with my little green watering can. It's this metal one with a copper spout that my wife bought me at a little hardware store up in Vermont on our anniversary trip maybe... oh, it must be ten or eleven years ago now. I'd be out there pinching off the little suckers between the branches and smelling that sharp, green tomato-leaf smell. I used to just love that smell. It used to be the absolute highlight of my day after coming home from the sorting carts at the library. But now? I look out the kitchen window from that oak table I told you about, and I see the weeds creeping up around the wire cages, and I just feel... nothing. I don't want to go out there. I don't look forward to the tomatoes ripening. I just let the weeds grow.

And it's the exact same story with my watercolors. I used to love Sunday mornings. My wife would make her coffee—she drinks that hazelnut blend, which I always thought smelled a bit too sweet, but she absolutely loves it—and she'd sit with her crossword, and I'd get out my heavy cold-pressed paper. I have this whole routine, you see. I tape down the edges with drafting tape so the paper doesn't warp when it gets wet, and I set up two glass jars of water, one for washing the paint off the brush and one for clean water so the colors don't get muddy on the page. I used to look forward to that all week long. Just the thought of laying down a nice, even wash of color for a sky... it gave me a little thrill, a sense of purpose. 

But now, the jars are bone dry. The tape is just sitting in the drawer. I look at my brushes and I just think, what's the point? It's just going to be a mess to clean up afterward, and I won't even enjoy the painting part. I don't feel that little spark of anticipation for any of it anymore. Even watching the evening news with my wife, which used to be our nice little wind-down ritual before bed... I just sit in my armchair, staring at the screen, just waiting for the half-hour to be over. So, no, doctor, I'm sorry to go on and on, but to answer your question, there really isn't anything at all right now that brings me that sense of pleasure. It's all just completely flat.
Have you ever wished you could just escape your current situation or find a way to make all these feelings stop?

Escape? Make it all stop? Well... no, doctor, I can't say that I have. 

I mean, I suppose everyone thinks about a nice vacation now and then. My wife—did I mention her name is Martha? We’ve been married thirty-five years this coming August, hard to believe how the time goes. Anyway, she sometimes sighs and says, "Oh, I wish we could just escape to the Cape for a week," you know, just to get away from the house and the usual routine. We used to rent this little cedar-shingled cottage up in Yarmouth, right near the water. It had these terrible drafty windows that rattled whenever the wind blew off the sound, but the screened-in porch was just lovely for reading. 

But... well, I know that's not what you mean, is it? You mean escaping in a more... permanent way. Or wanting to just throw my hands up and disappear because the feelings are too much. And no, I really don't have those sorts of thoughts at all. I know some people get so low they just want to pull the plug on everything, but that's just not me. Even with this... this heavy, gray blanket over everything, and sitting at that round oak table for hours just staring at my dry paint brushes like I told you, I don't want to escape. I don't sit there wishing I could just make it all stop by doing something drastic, or running away from my life. 

I just sit there. I suppose I'm just waiting for it to lift, really, the way a thick fog eventually lifts off the harbor. You just have to sit through it. I've always been a patient man, doctor. You have to be patient when you work at the library, especially with the filing systems and some of the newer clerks who always seem to put the historical biographies in the general fiction section. Oh, that drives Mrs. Gable absolutely up the wall, let me tell you, she gets red in the face. But you just have to breathe, and go through the cart, and fix it, one book at a time. 

So with this... this mood, I just take it one day at a time. I don't want to run away or make everything stop. I just want to get back to being myself, back to my watercolors and my tomato plants, eventually, whenever the fog decides to clear. So, no, no thoughts of escaping. Just... enduring it, I suppose you could say.
Are there any small pleasures in life that you still enjoy?

Well, doctor, I know we just talked about the tomatoes and the watercolors, which were my main hobbies, but if you mean the really, truly small things... the little moments in a day? I've been trying to find one, I really have. Because you'd think there would be something, wouldn't you? Just a tiny little spark somewhere to keep you going. 

Take my morning toast, for example. Every morning for, oh, it must be twenty years, I've had a piece of rye toast with this specific orange marmalade. We get it from a little farm stand out on Route 9. The fellow who runs it, Mr. Henderson, he always gives us a little discount because Martha used to teach his daughter in Sunday school—she was a lovely girl, played the cello, I believe, went off to a conservatory in Boston. Anyway, it’s a wonderful marmalade, got those thick rinds in it, just the right amount of bitter and sweet. I used to close my eyes and just savor that first bite. It was a perfect little quiet moment before I had to put on my coat and head down to the library to deal with the sorting carts and Mrs. Gable's fussing. 

But this morning? I sat at that round oak table, and I chewed my toast, and... nothing. I mean, my tongue knows it's sweet, I suppose, but there's absolutely no joy in it. It's just chewing and swallowing. Just fuel. Or the smell of the old books at work—I usually love that smell, especially in the historical archives section where the pages get that brittle, yellowed quality. It smells a bit like vanilla and dust, it's very comforting, usually. But when I was shelving yesterday, I just felt completely numb to it. I breathed it in and it was just... air. 

So, I'm afraid the answer is still no. Whether it's a big hobby like my painting or a tiny little thing like the marmalade on my toast, that gray blanket I mentioned just smothers it all. There just aren't any little pleasures getting through right now. None at all.
Have you been feeling anxious or nervous most days over the past three months?

Anxious? Nervous? Well... no, doctor, I really can't say that I have. 

It's funny you bring that up, though, because you'd think with everything feeling so heavy and wrong lately, I might be worried about it, or pacing the floors. But it's actually quite the opposite. I don't even have the energy to be nervous. 

Take Mrs. Gable down at the library, for instance. I mentioned her earlier, the one who gets so red in the face about the filing? Well, right now she is absolutely beside herself because the head librarian—that's Mr. Abernathy, he’s a younger fellow, only took over about three years ago when old Mr. Higgins finally retired and moved down to Boca Raton—anyway, Mr. Abernathy wants to switch our entire cataloging system over to some new computer software. Something about storing it all in the "cloud," which I don't pretend to fully understand, to be perfectly honest with you. Mrs. Gable has been in a total state for weeks. She’s convinced all the historical archive records are going to just vanish into thin air, and she’s running around the back office fluttering like a trapped bird, checking and re-checking the physical index cards. 

Normally, that kind of tension in the office might make me a bit on edge, you know? Just picking up on her nervous energy. I've always liked things to be calm and orderly, and usually, disruption makes me a little uneasy. But lately? Over these past few months since this fog rolled in? I just sit at my sorting cart, watching her panic, and I feel absolutely nothing. No nerves, no worry, no fluttering in my chest whatsoever. 

Martha even asked me last week—we were sitting in the living room, she was knitting this little yellow sweater for our niece's new baby, a boy, I think, or maybe they're keeping it a surprise, I can't quite recall—but she stopped her needles and asked if I was worried about something, if maybe the winter heating bills were making me anxious. And I had to tell her, Martha, I'm not worried about a single thing. 

I think you actually have to care about what happens next to feel nervous about it, don't you? You have to have some sort of stake in tomorrow to worry about it. And right now, under this heavy gray blanket... well, I just don't. It's perfectly still in my head. So, no, doctor, I haven't been anxious or nervous. Not at all. Just... flat.
Have you been feeling restless or having an urge to move around more than usual?

Restless? Oh, heavens no, doctor. Not in the slightest. It's... well, it's really quite the opposite, to be perfectly honest. 

If anything, my body just feels incredibly slow. It’s like I’m moving through wet cement, or molasses. Just the other day, Martha asked if I could pop down to the corner store. It’s just a little shop a few blocks over, run by the Garcias—lovely family, they’ve been in the neighborhood since the late nineties, and Mr. Garcia always makes sure to stock my favorite brand of decaf coffee. Anyway, Martha just needed a simple carton of milk for her tea. Normally, that walk takes me maybe five or six minutes, a nice little stroll past those big, old elm trees lining our street. But lately? Just putting on my winter boots and getting out the front door feels like I'm wearing lead weights. Every single step takes so much effort. Walking to that corner store felt like a marathon. I actually had to stop halfway there and lean against the brick wall of the old pharmacy building, not because I was out of breath, but because my legs just felt so impossibly heavy and slow. 

And it's the exact same thing at work. I mentioned my sorting cart earlier, and usually, my hands just fly through those returns, checking the spine labels, getting the Dewey Decimal numbers all lined up. It's second nature after all these years. But now... I stand there, and just sorting the papers on my desk—the daily logs, the inter-library loan slips—it takes more effort than it ever should. I just stare at my hands and wonder why they won't move the way they're supposed to. Even sliding a piece of paper into a folder feels like a monumental task. I watch Mrs. Gable darting around in her panic about the new computer system, and I couldn't replicate that kind of movement right now if my life depended on it. 

So, no, there's absolutely no urge to move around more than usual. I'd really rather not move at all if I could help it, because it's just so physically exhausting to get this slow body to do anything.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like headaches or muscle pains alongside your low mood?

Headaches? Muscle pains? Well... let me think about that for a moment. No, I really can't say that I do. I've always been quite fortunate with my health in that specific regard, to be perfectly honest. 

My older brother, Tom—he lives out in Ohio now, runs a hardware store out there—he gets these absolutely terrible migraines. Has since he was in his twenties. He used to have to go lie down in a completely dark room with a damp washcloth over his eyes for hours at a time, couldn't stand even a sliver of light coming in from the hallway. But me? I’ve just never been prone to them. Even now, with this whole heavy, gray feeling settling over everything, my head is perfectly clear of any actual pain. 

And as for the muscle aches... well, I am sixty years old, doctor, so I certainly won't sit here and tell you I never feel a twinge in my lower back. Especially if I've been lifting heavy boxes down at the archives. Just last month, actually, we had a massive donation of old National Geographic magazines—someone's entire basement collection from the nineteen-seventies—and you know how heavy that glossy paper can be. Moving those boxes onto the sorting carts gave me a bit of a stiff shoulder for a day or two. But that's just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It's just getting older. It has absolutely nothing to do with this... this mood I've been in. 

The slowness I mentioned earlier, the feeling like I'm moving through wet cement? It doesn't actually hurt. It's not an ache in the muscle or a sharp pain in the joints. It's just a profound heaviness. So, I suppose I should be thankful for small mercies, shouldn't I? If I had a pounding headache or aching bones on top of feeling this completely empty, I really don't know how I'd manage to get out of bed at all. But no, physically, aside from the sheer exhaustion of moving my limbs, nothing actually hurts.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?

Harming myself? Oh, my word, no. No, doctor, I haven't had any thoughts like that. Not at all. 

I know it's a standard question, and I suppose it makes sense that you have to ask, given how low I've been feeling. Martha actually... well, she hasn't asked me directly, but I can see it in her eyes sometimes. Just the other evening, we were sitting in the living room watching the local news—Channel 4, we always watch the six o'clock broadcast because Martha likes the weatherman, says he's the only one who gets the snow predictions right for our side of town—and there was a rather sad story on there. I won't go into the grim details, but I caught her looking over at me from her armchair with this terrible, worried expression. 

But I told her, and I'll tell you, it's just not something that crosses my mind. You see, I've always been a very cautious man by nature. Even down at the library, over in the genealogy section where the shelves go all the way up to those high vaulted ceilings, I won't even use the tall rolling ladders if I can help it. I've always been so careful about not getting hurt, about keeping things safe and predictable. 

And honestly, doctor, to do something like that... to actually harm yourself... I feel like you'd need to have some sort of sharp, active despair. A real piercing kind of agony, or a frantic need to escape. But like I was trying to explain earlier, with the wet cement and that heavy gray blanket over everything, there are no sharp edges to any of this. It’s all just completely dull and flat. It would take an immense amount of energy and planning to even conceptualize doing something to myself, and frankly, energy is the one thing I simply do not possess right now. 

I might not have much of a stake in tomorrow at the moment, and I might just want to sit perfectly still in my chair and not move a single muscle, but I wouldn't do anything to... to speed up the end of the book, so to speak. I just want to wait quietly and see if this fog eventually lifts. So, no. No thoughts of that nature whatsoever.
Would you describe your current low mood as mild, moderate, or severe?

Well... mild, moderate, severe. That’s a tricky way to measure it, isn't it? I suppose if I had to pick one of those three words, I would probably go with moderate. It's certainly not mild, because it's not just a passing case of the blues that goes away after a good night's sleep or a nice cup of tea. But I wouldn't call it severe, either, because like I was just saying, I'm not in any sort of frantic, unbearable agony, and I'm still managing to get myself to work, even if it takes everything out of me. 

It’s more of a... well, a pervasive dullness. To give you an idea of what I mean, most days lately, I just sit at our kitchen table. It’s this sturdy old oak table Martha and I found at an antique fair out in Lancaster County nearly thirty years ago—beautiful claw feet on it, very heavy wood. Anyway, I’ll just sit there, staring out the window or at the wall, and it honestly feels like the color has just completely gone out of everything. The whole world, my whole life, it all just looks washed out and gray. 

I have these old watercolor books, you see. Books I've kept for years, filled with little sketches and paintings I’ve done of the neighborhood, or the birds that visit our feeder out back—cardinals, blue jays, the occasional goldfinch. I used to spend hours on a Sunday morning just getting my brushes wet and mixing the pigments, trying to get the exact shade of a winter sky or the green of the elm leaves. It was such a quiet joy for me. But now... Martha will set the books out on the table for me, right next to my coffee cup, bless her heart. She thinks it might spark something, remind me of what I enjoy. But I look at them, and even my old watercolor books just make me feel heavy instead of interested. 

There’s absolutely no spark there anymore. I don't want to open them, I don't want to look at the colors I painted, because I just can't feel them. The thought of even picking up a brush just adds to that terrible weight I was telling you about earlier. So, yes, a very heavy, moderate sort of grayness. I think moderate is probably the most accurate word for it.
Have you noticed any change in the intensity of your low mood over the past three months?

Change in intensity? Over the past three months... well, let me just think back on that for a moment. 

Three months ago would put us right around... oh, I suppose the middle of November. Right before Thanksgiving. Martha always insists on getting a fresh turkey from that farm out on Route 9, you know, the one with the big red silo? We've been going there for nearly two decades. And I remember feeling this exact same way when we drove out there to pick it up this year. Just... incredibly heavy. I remember sitting in the passenger seat watching the bare trees go by, and I felt like I was made of lead. 

And since then? Through December, and the holidays, and all that bitter cold we had in January... no, I really can't say it's fluctuated at all. It hasn't gotten worse, which I suppose is a blessing, because I honestly don't know if I could manage if this wet-cement feeling got any thicker. But it certainly hasn't lightened up, not even a fraction of an inch. 

It's actually very strange how time works when you feel like this. I look at the calendar on our kitchen wall—Martha gets one every year from the local savings bank, the ones with the pictures of old New England covered bridges for every month—and I watch the weeks get crossed off, but every single day just feels like one long, continuous gray afternoon. Tuesday feels exactly like Saturday, and December felt exactly like February. target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My body feels slow, like even walking to the corner store or sorting papers on my desk takes more effort than it should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restlessness or the urge to move around, which relates to psychomotor agitation. This falls under the symptom of psychomotor changes, which in my profile manifests as feeling slow and heavy (psychomotor retardation).

patient.answer:
Restless? Oh, heavens no, doctor. Not in the slightest. It's... well, it's really quite the opposite, to be perfectly honest. 

If anything, my body just feels incredibly slow. It’s like I’m moving through wet cement, or molasses. Just the other day, Martha asked if I could pop down to the corner store. It’s just a little shop a few blocks over, run by the Garcias—lovely family, they’ve been in the neighborhood since the late nineties, and Mr. Garcia always makes sure to stock my favorite brand of decaf coffee. Anyway, Martha just needed a simple carton of milk for her tea. Normally, that walk takes me maybe five or six minutes, a nice little stroll past those big, old elm trees lining our street. But lately? Just putting on my winter boots and getting out the front door feels like I'm wearing lead weights. Every single step takes so much effort. Walking to that corner store felt like a marathon. I actually had to stop halfway there and lean against the brick wall of the old pharmacy building, not because I was out of breath, but because my legs just felt so impossibly heavy and slow. 

And it's the exact same thing at work. I mentioned my sorting cart earlier, and usually, my hands just fly through those returns, checking the spine labels, getting the Dewey Decimal numbers all lined up. It's second nature after all these years. But now... I stand there, and just sorting the papers on my desk—the daily logs, the inter-library loan slips—it takes more effort than it ever should. I just stare at my hands and wonder why they won't move the way they're supposed to. Even sliding a piece of paper into a folder feels like a monumental task. I watch Mrs. Gable darting around in her panic about the new computer system, and I couldn't replicate that kind of movement right now if my life depended on it. 

So, no, there's absolutely no urge to move around more than usual. I'd really rather not move at all if I could help it, because it's just so physically exhausting to get this slow body to do anything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for F32.0 (Mild depressive episode) or F32.1 (Moderate depressive episode) based on the presence of somatic symptoms
doctor.question: Do you experience any physical symptoms like headaches or muscle pains alongside your low mood?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms such as headaches or muscle pains, which are not covered by any of the available symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Headaches? Muscle pains? Well... let me think about that for a moment. No, I really can't say that I do. I've always been quite fortunate with my health in that specific regard, to be perfectly honest. 

My older brother, Tom—he lives out in Ohio now, runs a hardware store out there—he gets these absolutely terrible migraines. Has since he was in his twenties. He used to have to go lie down in a completely dark room with a damp washcloth over his eyes for hours at a time, couldn't stand even a sliver of light coming in from the hallway. But me? I’ve just never been prone to them. Even now, with this whole heavy, gray feeling settling over everything, my head is perfectly clear of any actual pain. 

And as for the muscle aches... well, I am sixty years old, doctor, so I certainly won't sit here and tell you I never feel a twinge in my lower back. Especially if I've been lifting heavy boxes down at the archives. Just last month, actually, we had a massive donation of old National Geographic magazines—someone's entire basement collection from the nineteen-seventies—and you know how heavy that glossy paper can be. Moving those boxes onto the sorting carts gave me a bit of a stiff shoulder for a day or two. But that's just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It's just getting older. It has absolutely nothing to do with this... this mood I've been in. 

The slowness I mentioned earlier, the feeling like I'm moving through wet cement? It doesn't actually hurt. It's not an ache in the muscle or a sharp pain in the joints. It's just a profound heaviness. So, I suppose I should be thankful for small mercies, shouldn't I? If I had a pounding headache or aching bones on top of feeling this completely empty, I really don't know how I'd manage to get out of bed at all. But no, physically, aside from the sheer exhaustion of moving my limbs, nothing actually hurts.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Harming myself? Oh, my word, no. No, doctor, I haven't had any thoughts like that. Not at all. 

I know it's a standard question, and I suppose it makes sense that you have to ask, given how low I've been feeling. Martha actually... well, she hasn't asked me directly, but I can see it in her eyes sometimes. Just the other evening, we were sitting in the living room watching the local news—Channel 4, we always watch the six o'clock broadcast because Martha likes the weatherman, says he's the only one who gets the snow predictions right for our side of town—and there was a rather sad story on there. I won't go into the grim details, but I caught her looking over at me from her armchair with this terrible, worried expression. 

But I told her, and I'll tell you, it's just not something that crosses my mind. You see, I've always been a very cautious man by nature. Even down at the library, over in the genealogy section where the shelves go all the way up to those high vaulted ceilings, I won't even use the tall rolling ladders if I can help it. I've always been so careful about not getting hurt, about keeping things safe and predictable. 

And honestly, doctor, to do something like that... to actually harm yourself... I feel like you'd need to have some sort of sharp, active despair. A real piercing kind of agony, or a frantic need to escape. But like I was trying to explain earlier, with the wet cement and that heavy gray blanket over everything, there are no sharp edges to any of this. It’s all just completely dull and flat. It would take an immense amount of energy and planning to even conceptualize doing something to myself, and frankly, energy is the one thing I simply do not possess right now. 

I might not have much of a stake in tomorrow at the moment, and I might just want to sit perfectly still in my chair and not move a single muscle, but I wouldn't do anything to... to speed up the end of the book, so to speak. I just want to wait quietly and see if this fog eventually lifts. So, no. No thoughts of that nature whatsoever.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depressive episode
doctor.question: Would you describe your current low mood as mild, moderate, or severe?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days lately I sit at the kitchen table feeling like the color has gone out of everything, and even my old watercolor books just make me feel heavy instead of interested.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the severity of my current low mood, which directly relates to my depressed mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well... mild, moderate, severe. That’s a tricky way to measure it, isn't it? I suppose if I had to pick one of those three words, I would probably go with moderate. It's certainly not mild, because it's not just a passing case of the blues that goes away after a good night's sleep or a nice cup of tea. But I wouldn't call it severe, either, because like I was just saying, I'm not in any sort of frantic, unbearable agony, and I'm still managing to get myself to work, even if it takes everything out of me. 

It’s more of a... well, a pervasive dullness. To give you an idea of what I mean, most days lately, I just sit at our kitchen table. It’s this sturdy old oak table Martha and I found at an antique fair out in Lancaster County nearly thirty years ago—beautiful claw feet on it, very heavy wood. Anyway, I’ll just sit there, staring out the window or at the wall, and it honestly feels like the color has just completely gone out of everything. The whole world, my whole life, it all just looks washed out and gray. 

I have these old watercolor books, you see. Books I've kept for years, filled with little sketches and paintings I’ve done of the neighborhood, or the birds that visit our feeder out back—cardinals, blue jays, the occasional goldfinch. I used to spend hours on a Sunday morning just getting my brushes wet and mixing the pigments, trying to get the exact shade of a winter sky or the green of the elm leaves. It was such a quiet joy for me. But now... Martha will set the books out on the table for me, right next to my coffee cup, bless her heart. She thinks it might spark something, remind me of what I enjoy. But I look at them, and even my old watercolor books just make me feel heavy instead of interested. 

There’s absolutely no spark there anymore. I don't want to open them, I don't want to look at the colors I painted, because I just can't feel them. The thought of even picking up a brush just adds to that terrible weight I was telling you about earlier. So, yes, a very heavy, moderate sort of grayness. I think moderate is probably the most accurate word for it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is improving or worsening over time
doctor.question: Have you noticed any change in the intensity of your low mood over the past three months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the trajectory or change in intensity of the low mood over the past three months. While there is a 'duration' (3 weeks) and 'depressive_episode_duration' (3 months) in the symptom profile, they do not specifically address whether the intensity of the mood has changed over time. The 'Depressed_Mood' symptom describes the nature of the mood, but not its change in intensity.

patient.answer:
Change in intensity? Over the past three months... well, let me just think back on that for a moment. 

Three months ago would put us right around... oh, I suppose the middle of November. Right before Thanksgiving. Martha always insists on getting a fresh turkey from that farm out on Route 9, you know, the one with the big red silo? We've been going there for nearly two decades. And I remember feeling this exact same way when we drove out there to pick it up this year. Just... incredibly heavy. I remember sitting in the passenger seat watching the bare trees go by, and I felt like I was made of lead. 

And since then? Through December, and the holidays, and all that bitter cold we had in January... no, I really can't say it's fluctuated at all. It hasn't gotten worse, which I suppose is a blessing, because I honestly don't know if I could manage if this wet-cement feeling got any thicker. But it certainly hasn't lightened up, not even a fraction of an inch. 

It's actually very strange how time works when you feel like this. I look at the calendar on our kitchen wall—Martha gets one every year from the local savings bank, the ones with the pictures of old New England covered bridges for every month—and I watch the weeks get crossed off, but every single day just feels like one long, continuous gray afternoon. Tuesday feels exactly like Saturday, and December felt exactly like February. I go to the library, I do my sorting and filing, I come home, I sit at that oak table... and the weight of it all is exactly the same today as it was ninety days ago. 

So, no, doctor. No change in the intensity. It hasn't dipped and it hasn't peaked. It's just been a very steady, very stubborn flatline this whole time.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts without the energy to act on them
doctor.question: Do you have any thoughts of self-harm that you don't have the energy to carry out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of self-harm, which is not covered by any item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, I see. I understand the distinction you're making, doctor. You're wondering if the... the dark ideas are brewing up there, but I'm just too bogged down to actually do anything about them. But no, I can assure you, it really isn't like that at all. The thoughts themselves simply do not exist in my head. 

It’s a very specific kind of emptiness, you see. When I'm sitting at that oak table I mentioned, or when I'm at the circulation desk down at the library—which, by the way, the head librarian decided to move closer to the drafty front vestibule last month, so now I have to wear my thick wool cardigan just to sit there and process the return slips—my mind isn't churning with morbid plans or anything of that nature. I'm not sitting there wishing I could hurt myself but feeling too exhausted to get up and do it. 

If I had to compare it to something, it's sort of like... well, like a movie theater where the projector has just been completely unplugged. There isn't a scary or sad movie playing that I'm just too tired to watch. The screen is just entirely blank. I just sit there feeling that heavy grayness. The idea of harming myself simply doesn't materialize in the first place. 

And I suppose I'm very grateful for that, because Martha, she worries enough as it is just seeing me stare into space. If I were actually harboring those kinds of dangerous thoughts, even silently, even without the energy to act on them, I truly believe she would sense it. We've been married long enough that she can read my silences, if that makes sense. She knows the difference between me being quiet because I'm thinking about a book, and me being quiet because I'm... well, stuck in the mud. So, no, it's a very fair question for you to ask, but I can honestly tell you that the thoughts themselves just aren't there, regardless of how little energy I have.
